newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House panel told NAFTA not working.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House panel told NAFTA not working.

text.p: A House panel was told Wednesday that the North American Free Trade Agreement was not working and should not be expanded to include Chile until it is fixed.
"I believe for the most part NAFTA has been an utter failure," Rep. David Bonior, the second ranking Democrat in the House, told the House International Relations subcommittee.
"Expanding NAFTA now would be like building a new room onto your house when your kitchen is on fire and your roof is collapsing," he said.

Bonior, of Michigan, is one of 41 co-sponsors of a bill introduced in the House by Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, on Wednesday that would require President Clinton to certify that the trade accord is working as promised or, if not, renegotiate it.
The bill would not allow NAFTA to be expanded until the terms were met.
It is similiar to legislation introduced last year that gained 110 supporters. Sponsors of the new measure said at a news conference that they expect even more support this year.
Bonior noted that the House now has more members who voted against the agreement, which joins Canada the United States and Mexico in a trade bloc, than voted for it.
Rep. Duncan Hunter, R-Calif., said that many lawmakers who supported the greement, which was ratified by the U.S. Congress in 1993 by a slim margin, are reconsidering their support for the agreement.

The anti-NAFTA forces building in Congress underscore the difficulty President Clinton faces in trying to get so-called "fast track" trade negotiating authority that would allow him to make a deal with Chile to bring it into NAFTA.
Chile was invited in 1994 to negotiate entry into the trading bloc, but talks with the United States have been delayed by a lack of fast track trade negotiation authority.

Rep. Pat Danner, D-Mo., a member of the House panel that held Wednesday's hearing on NAFTA, said during the session that several hundred jobs have been lost in her district because companies closed their plants and moved to Mexico.
"I can't find any evidence at all of anything that has been a plus in my district from NAFTA," she said.
Subcommittee Chairwomman Lleana Ros-Lehtinen, R-Fla., said that NAFTA may not be living up to everything promised by its supporters.

"Serious deficiencies in the agreement have continued to afford Mexico a comparative advantage over the United States by maintaining a low wage strategy, coupled with weak environmental, health and safety standards," she said.
Oppenents of NAFTA say that hundreds of thousands of U.S. jobs have been lost because of the agreement.

But Senior U.S. Trade Representative negotiator Ira Shapiro, pointing to more than 8 million new jobs created in the United States in the last four years, said estimtes of NAFTA job losses were exaggerated.
"Rather, the evidence shows that the NAFTA has contributed to the strength of our economy," he said.
He told reporters after the hearing that the administration was working with lawmakers on a proposed fast track trade bill and expected to send a proposed bill to Congress "in the coming weeks."
The legislation would allow U.S. trade officials to negotiate trade agreements without fear they would later be changed by lawmakers. Congress would vote either "yes" or "no" on the agreement.
